TEXT — edit this column: Pick it up. It is only paper.
You bend down and take it. The warmth on your face is suddenly gone.
What is burned is already given. Take it away, and the debt returns in another form.
Kick it and laugh. Superstition is for other people.
Your foot scuffs across the concrete. Behind you, something is on the chase.
You do not have to believe in something to respect it. Disrespect may invite what belief never could.
Stop and look around before walking away.
Your intuition was right. This is not a place for you to be standing.
Observation costs nothing and prevents the unintended. Awareness is the cheapest protection there is.
Recite a chant, then respectfully excuse yourself.
The lamp buzzes. A sense of peacefulness arise.
Act wisely. Respect what you cannot see. It may matter more than you think.

The Worst Bed
Bed One, Next To The Toilet
Day one of Basic Military Training. Twenty recruits to a bunk, and yours is the bottom bed nearest the toilet door. Nobody wanted it. Get through the day; then get through the night.
Three in the morning. The shower in the block next to your bed has turned itself on. What do you do?

A sound is a fact. What made it is a story you have not checked.
Sati — bare attention, before the mind adds its tale.
FALL IN — on the yellow line
FALL IN — get to the line
Back to your bed — standby bed
Stand by your bed — wait for orders
STANDBY BED — lay it out, fast
Drag each item on the left onto its place on the right. The faster you lay the whole set out, the better it is inspected — and every item put in the wrong place costs you.
Look around the bunk before lights out
Lights out is coming — get to your bed
The bunk did it again because of you.
Get up and open the toilet door.
I got up and looked. I found water, and nothing else, and a corridor I did not like.
Investigating can provide information, but moving straight toward uncertainty is not automatically the wisest first step.
I stayed still and listened. What I heard was a sound. What it meant, I did not know yet.
Hearing something frightening is an observation. Deciding what caused it is an interpretation.
I asked the one person who could tell me. He heard nothing. That was worth knowing.
Check simple human explanations before building a more complicated interpretation.
It's a ghost — blanket over your head.
I decided what it was before I knew anything. Under the blanket, the water kept running.
Fear is a signal, not proof.
Days later. Your own bedroom, the fan turning, the streetlight coming through the window. Someone has been crying in this flat and it is not your mother. Tonight the room is not empty.
Something is in the gap between the bed and the wall. What do you do?
Know the edge of what you can handle. You do not have to suffer in silence.
Something is not right in here...
E at the gap beside the bed
tap the gap beside the bed
Look into the gap beside the bed
You lean over the edge and look down into the dark. It is looking back, and it has been for a while.
Awareness can reveal more, but investigation without preparation has a cost.
You shout. Nothing. Then a door, and slippers shuffles in, and the light.
Seeking help is not weakness. Knowing your limits is part of wisdom.
You decide to head out. At the door you look back, and the room looks ordinary.
Creating distance can reduce exposure even if it does not solve the cause.
Stay silent and do not move.
You lie still and count the fan going round. Beside your head, the mattress takes someone’s weight.
Stillness may prevent escalation, but enduring fear is not the same as solving the problem.
Night after night, at three in the morning, the shower beside bed one turns itself on. This morning you have decided to say something. Ask three bunkmates what they heard. Then tell the encik.
The encik is watching the recruits eat. You have asked three men. Now you are standing in front of him. What do you say?

What you say about a thing becomes what is known about it. Say what you know — not less, and not more.
Sammā vācā — right speech: true, useful, and in its time.
E to speak to the encik
Tap to speak to the encik
E to speak to the encik
Tap to speak to the encik
Ask three bunkmates what they heard · {n}/3
"Encik, something happened. I don't know what."
I told him what I knew, and only that. He didn't laugh.
Document before interpreting. Wisdom can include: I don't know yet.
"Encik, the bunk is haunted. I'm sure."
I said I was sure. I wasn't. Now nobody will listen.
Confirmation bias can make ordinary events feel like proof.
"Never mind encik, I think I was just tired."
I called it nothing. It wasn't nothing. Three a.m. knew that.
Scepticism is not the same as dismissal.
"Encik, what do you think it is?"
He gave me three answers and one rule. The rule was the answer.
Good guidance expands your thinking; it does not replace your judgement.

The tentage has been up all week in the car park under his block. This morning there is a drum, a crowd on red plastic chairs, and a man at the altar who has stopped being himself. Everyone is watching the front. Nobody is watching row four.
The medium has gone into trance at the altar. What do you do?
Some things lie beyond understanding. Keep an open mind, and observe before you judge.
The whole tent is watching the front...
Watch the ritual at the altar
Stay at the back and watch.
You stay at the back and watch it unfold. You've never seen anything like this before.
You go up with the others. The drum is inside your chest, the air goes thin, and someone takes your arm and walks you out of it.
Participation increases exposure. Do not enter practices you do not yet understand.
Ask the auntie what is happening.
She does not laugh at you. She tells you what the man is doing, and what he is not. Then she tells you where not to sit.
Questioning respectfully is part of discernment.
You are out before the drum stops. It is quieter out here, and that turns out to be worse.
Leaving can be appropriate when you lack the knowledge to engage safely.

Back Home
It Knows Where I Live

The evening after the tentage. You stayed out all day, and now the sun is down and there is nowhere left to go but home. Ma is working late. The flat is empty, the lights are on, and none of that helps.
You know something is following you. What do you do about it, tonight?

A pattern seen clearly is half the answer.
Yoniso manasikāra — wise attention to how things arise.
The flat is too quiet tonight...
Sit down and think it through
You review the sequence. A pattern begins to emerge. The events no longer feel random.
Look for patterns before jumping to conclusions. Context matters.
You convince yourself nothing is wrong and try to sleep. You wake later to the same unsettling atmosphere.
Dismissal is not discernment. Repeated warning signs deserve careful assessment.
The environment reacts violently. Provocation added danger without giving understanding.
Never provoke what you do not understand merely to prove that it exists.
You stop trying to handle this alone. Help is coming tomorrow. Tonight, mom's voice is enough.
Knowing when to seek qualified guidance is a form of wisdom.

The Lesson
What It Was All For
Morning. Ma is home, the tea is poured, and the tang-ki from the tentage is standing in the living room reading the flat like a letter. On the table: the hell note. It was here all along.
The tang-ki has read every room, and the hellnote lies on the table. What do you ask of him?

Do not dismiss. Do not provoke. Observe, and seek knowledge before acting.
The first case is closed. The lesson is yours to keep.
He walks the flat like he is reading it...
You sit down with him and ask what you should learn from everything that happened. Fear has given way to wisdom.
Do not assume. Do not provoke. Observe, understand the situation and seek guidance before acting.
Ignore him and trust your fear alone.
Fear begins filling in the missing information before you verify what is actually there.
Always verify before deciding what something means.
You decide it must have been imagination and refuse to examine further. You lose what it was trying to teach.
Blind disbelief can be as unhelpful as blind belief. Discernment requires real observation and an open mind.
Ask him to settle the presence.
You accept that you do not understand everything yet, and commit to learning without recklessness. The note is returned to the fire. The case becomes your first lesson.
Wisdom grows when experience is combined with humility, observation and proper guidance.
